canberra.title: Online enforcement register allows parents to make more informed childcare choices
canberra.snippet: Enforcement activities taken against Canberra childcare centres can be accessed by the public from Monday (30 November) under the creatio...
canberra.content:
29 November 2026

Start the conversation

Parents will now be able to see just what enforcement activities are being taken against Canberra’s childcare centres. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Enforcement activities taken against Canberra childcare centres can be accessed by the public from Monday (30 November) under the creation of a new online register.

The Enforcement Action Register will provide a high-level overview of activities being undertaken by the independent regulator, Children’s Education and Care Assurance (CECA).

The details published will include the service’s name, the date of action, the type and reason for the enforcement, and a summary of the actions required to be demonstrated by the service.

“The Enforcement Action Register will help families make more informed decisions about their child’s early education and care,” Child Development and Wellbeing Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said.

“The register will provide additional transparency and accountability for children, families and educators themselves, while we continue supporting the sector to provide the highest quality of early education and care possible.”

The initial register will include publishable actions issued from 1 January 2026.

It will continue to be updated quarterly, with entries to remain online for two years from their publication date.

Education and Care Regulation and Support executive branch manager Sean Moysey said the information would only contain what CECA was permitted to publish under law.

“It complements information available through Starting Blocks and helps families and the community understand CECA’s regulatory activity,” he said.

“It also supports national child safety reforms that strengthen oversight, accountability and transparency across the early childhood education and care sector.”

Information published by CECA will be subject to legal, privacy and quality assurance checks. It won’t identify, or lead to the identification of, a child or an educator.

Ms Stephen-Smith said protecting educator identities was important.

“This isn’t about naming and shaming educators who make a mistake or who are let down by a lack of proper systems and supports,” she said.

“The reality is that committed, skilled educators are our best asset when it comes to keeping children safe, and we see this every day across dozens of services in the ACT.”

Independent Kurrajong MLA Thomas Emerson had pushed for more transparency around actions being taken against Canberra’s childcare centres and providers.

He’s also called for an online register to check the validity of Working With Vulnerable People cards and making it possible for CECA to actually fine centres who breach standards, among other calls.

Earlier this year Mr Emerson had expressed his hope that real change was coming to the early childhood education sector to better protect children, parents and workers.

“The fact is we have a system that’s not currently set up to support and incentivise best practice when it comes to the education and care of children,” Mr Emerson said.

“We can’t just put our head in the sand and pretend that there aren’t issues.

“We have an opportunity to turn that around.”

The Enforcement Action Register can be found online.

canberra.title: Meet the makers and try before you buy at Canberra’s Biggest Christmas Cellar Door
canberra.snippet: If you were inspired by the recent results of the Canberra Region Wine Show, where our cool-climate winemakers showed off their best asse...
canberra.content:
The winemakers of the Canberra district are preparing for Canberra’s Biggest Cellar Door at The Vault. Photo: Nathan Brown, Linear Wines.

If you were inspired by the recent results of the Canberra Region Wine Show, where our cool-climate winemakers showed off their best assets, then Canberra’s Biggest Christmas Cellar Door should be on your radar.

At Dairy Road’s The Vault on 6 December, you can expect a gathering of 17 of Canberra District’s finest winemakers and distillers, all keen to help you nail your Christmas shopping in a fun, festive environment where the wine will flow.

Hosted by the Canberra Wine District Collective, the admission fee at the door is $10, and you’ll be handed a wine glass to take home and an invitation to wander the floor in a format that lets you try before you buy.

Event committee member Carla Rodeghiero of Sapling Yard Wines says the event is designed to make Christmas shopping something people actually look forward to.

“Bring your list, taste a few wines and have a chat with the people who made them.”

Carla Rodeghiero of Sapling Yard Wines is excited to join her winemaking friends and bring their knowledge and award-winning wines to Canberra Christmas tables. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Carla says it will not only be ideal for those looking for gifts, especially those that are hard to buy for, but with some of the best winemakers in the region all in one place, you’ll be able to get advice on wine pairings for the Christmas table.

The winemaking community in the Canberra region is surprisingly close-knit, with Carla explaining that they all champion each other’s awards and achievements.

Carla says the diversity of Canberra’s wine scene makes an event like this a real drawcard, bringing favourite producers together in one place and giving visitors a chance to reduce their Christmas shopping kilometres without missing out.

Attendees can take home their tasting glass and enjoy all the fun of visiting a cellar door, but on a bigger scale. Photo: Belinda Pratten, Mount Majura Vineyard.

In the true spirit of the cellar door, Carla says that there will be cheese and charcuterie available, plus a handful of food vendors, so people can settle in and make an occasion out of it, with a lucky door prize up for grabs, sending someone home with a case of local wine.

Among the winemakers in attendance, you’ll find Sapling Yard, of course, with owner and winemaker Carla having hatched the idea for the event. They’ll be bringing their Wamboin-based wines, which were recognised with 16 medals at the recent Canberra Region Wine Show.

Gundog Estate will be there with Canberra district’s best Riesling. If you’re into Tempranillo, Nathan Brown will be attending with his label, Linear Wines, which was awarded Best Tempranillo, and Mada Wines, hot off their win for best dry white, will be there too.

The remaining attendees, all celebrated winemakers of the region, read like a best-of-the-best list, with Barton Estate, Capital Wines, Enotria, Four Winds, Lerida, Mount Majura, Norton Road, Pankhurst, Quarry Hill, Sassafras and Shaw Wines all bringing their popular drops.

Canberra’s Biggest Cellar Door will be taking place on Sunday 6 December at The Vault, 1 Dairy Road, Fyshwick. The event kicks off at 11 am and wraps up at 4 pm, with $10 admission at the door, which includes a take-home wine glass and an invitation to mingle, taste and shop.
Exclusive discounts will be available from winemakers on the day.

canberra.title: Canberra Liberals lose another MLA as Peter Cain quits, becomes independent
canberra.snippet: Ginninderra MLA Peter Cain has quit the Canberra Liberals to now represent the community as an independent. As part of the announcement, ...
canberra.content:
Gininderra MLA Peter Cain will finish up the rest of this term as in independent, and has already announced he’ll contest the 2028 ACT election. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Ginninderra MLA Peter Cain has quit the Canberra Liberals to now represent the community as an independent.

As part of the announcement, he seemed to imply more instability behind the scenes, stating sitting alone would give him more freedom.

“Public office is a responsibility, not a privilege. My foremost obligation is to the people who elected me and the proper governance of our Territory,” Mr Cain said.

“After 25 years of Labor government, Canberra urgently needs greater transparency, stronger financial discipline and better essential services.

“The growing distance between what this government promises, what it spends and what it delivers should concern every Canberran.”

“I believe I can pursue these issues more effectively and freely as an Independent.”

He’s the second person to quit the Canberra Liberals during this term of government.

Leanne Castley left the party in June after alleging she had been the subject of bullying and that the party had a toxic culture.

Mr Cain said he “remained grateful” to his parliamentary colleagues, and the Canberra Liberals MLAs and staff who had supported him.

“My values have not changed. What is changing is the freedom with which I can act upon them,” he said.

Mr Cain outlined his immediate priorities as:

  • Challenging government secrecy and reforming freedom of information, public disclosure
    and parliamentary accountability
  • Prioritising frontline services over unnecessary bureaucracy
  • Strengthening scrutiny of procurement, conflicts of interest and senior public sector
    accountability
  • Restoring discipline to the Territory’s finances and public expenditure
  • Developing constructive policy alternatives to address Canberra’s long-term challenges

“Canberrans are entitled to a government that answers questions, accepts accountability for its decisions, and spends responsibly,” he said.

“I will use every parliamentary mechanism available to pursue those standards, wherever the evidence leads and without seeking political permission.”

He also promised to keep the Belconnen area central to his parliamentary work.

“From Margaret Timpson Park, Hawker Tennis Centre, and Big Splash, to library opening hours and local infrastructure, Belconnen residents deserve more than assurances. They deserve outcomes,” he said.

“Independence does not mean opposition for opposition’s sake. I will support sound proposals wherever they originate, challenge poor decisions with evidence and put forward constructive alternatives.”

Mr Cain will be spending the next two years developing his own agenda and policies, confirming he will run as an independent in the 2028 ACT election.

“Should my support be sought to form a government after that election, meaningful commitments to those reforms will be a condition of that support,” he said.

“Ultimately, this is a question of duty. The Barr Government must be held systematically and relentlessly to account.

“I remain dedicated to quality services for my constituents, indeed for all residents of Canberra, and committed to holding the government accountable for its promises and actions.

“Over the next 22 and a half months, it is my plan, and my hope, to improve as many lives, and circumstances, of Canberrans as I possibly can, especially those living in my Electorate.”

Opposition Leader Mark Parton said Mr Cain’s departure said more about the man than it did about the Canberra Liberals.

“The Canberra Liberals are disappointed by Peter Cain’s decision to leave the party and sit as an independent,” he said.

“Peter was elected to the Assembly as a Canberra Liberal in 2020 and again in 2024. The people of Ginninderra voted for a Canberra Liberal, and that is the mandate on which he was elected on.

“Peter’s decision came as a surprise.”

Mr Parton said the decision wouldn’t be a distraction to the Canberra Liberals MLAs who remained behind.

“Our team is focused and getting on with what Canberrans expect of us, which is holding this government to account and offering a real alternative in 2028,” he said.

“This also gives us the chance to refresh our representation in Ginninderra. Belconnen deserves a strong, Canberra Liberals team, and we will be putting forward candidates who are ready to fight for it in 2028.

“The Canberra Liberals remain committed to the people of Belconnen and to offering Canberrans a real alternative at the next election.”

It will make for an even more interesting final sitting week, which begins on Tuesday (1 December).

canberra.title: Call to cut e-bike and scooter speeds on Canberra paths
canberra.snippet: The speed limit for electric bikes and scooters on shared paths should be cut from 25 km/h to 15 km/h in light of a growing death and inj...
canberra.content:
E-scooter and e-bike use is accelerating in Canberra. Photo: ACT Government.

The speed limit for electric bikes and scooters on shared paths should be cut from 25 km/h to 15 km/h in light of a growing death and injury toll as their take-up accelerates, a Canberra community council has urged.

Inner South Canberra Community Council Colin Walters has written to the ACT Government and made a submission to the ACCC, calling for the reduction in speed limit and supporting the ACCC’s push for e-bikes to be pegged at a maximum power-assisted speed of 25 km/h.

Mr Walters said that the current 15 km/h limit on footpaths should be cut to just 10 km/h, and e-bikes should be capable of emitting a warning sound.

Those with comparable speeds to petrol-powered motorbikes and scooters should be subject to the same licensing requirements and age limits.

Mr Walters said that smaller e-bikes aimed at the young teenage market should have a lower maximum speed.

“Smaller but powerful e-bikes are being marketed to younger teenagers, who are increasingly seen riding in groups on our paths and in our parks,” he said.

Delivery drivers riding e-bikes carrying large food containers also increased the risk of injury in a collision with pedestrians.

Mr Walters said sections of Canberra’s path network were already at capacity with cyclists, runners and walkers.

He said e-bike riders regularly flouted existing laws with apparent impunity and called for authorities to crack down on breaches.

There did not appear to be any serious enforcement of laws, including helmet use and the ban on more than one person per bike.

Hired e-bikes should not be exempt from any new rules.

Mr Walters said speed mattered, and is directly related to the seriousness of injuries in any collision.

“We regularly observe irresponsible behaviour by users of e-bikes, the dangers from which are greatly increased by the 25 km/h limit available on Canberra’s shared paths,” Mr Walters said.

“The energy involved when a pedestrian is hit by an e-bike travelling at 25 km/h rather than 15 km/h is 278 per cent more energetic, almost three times more damaging.

“The likely consequences of rapidly increasing e-bike usage, alongside the existing speed limit on shared paths which are already often at maximum capacity, including vulnerable users such as the elderly and young children, are increasing injuries and deaths, with more pressure on emergency services.”

Mr Walters said the risks were only increasing, with e-bike and scooter sales surging, as well as Lime operating in Canberra.

He said market reports say that Australia is projected to sell between 250,000 and 300,000 e-bikes a year, with the market entering a period of sustained double-digit growth.

A University of Melbourne study identified 37 fatal e-scooter incidents nationally between 2020 and 2025 — more than one in three involved a child under 18.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare reported that “hospitalisation rates in Australia for falls involving powered scooters have tripled since 2019-20, reaching 15 per 100,000 population in 2024–25. The number of in-hospital deaths among people hospitalised for falls involving powered scooters increased from seven in 2015-16 to 20 in 2024-25″.

“We are already seeing far too many accidents and near misses involving e-bikes and e-scooters,” Mr Walters said.

“The elderly and disabled are particularly vulnerable pedestrians.

“Accidents will soon reach epidemic proportions given the current growth rate in sales. The time for the government to act is now, before the problem gets out of hand”.

ACT Policing said last month, in response to the AIHW report, that police were not notified of every incident involving e-bikes and e-scooters, so the true scale of the problem was unknown. Often people injured were treated in hospital without police action being required.

Most riders did the right thing, but police remain concerned about poor behaviour. In February this year, a 12-year-old boy was seriously injured in a collision between an e-bike and a car in Melba. The boy was one of three riding the e-bike.

Most fines were for not wearing a helmet, and police were also concerned about illegal modifications to e-bikes or e-scooters, which leave riders legally liable if they injure someone.

canberra.title: $38 for four cookies? Canberra’s Instagram-famous Munchies live up to the hype
canberra.snippet: What’s the most you’ve ever paid for some cookies? Until last week, for me, it was probably $5. For a pack of Tim Tams. Tim T...
canberra.content:
“Freaking good cookies”. ‘Nuff said. Photo: Munchies.

What’s the most you’ve ever paid for some cookies? Until last week, for me, it was probably $5. For a pack of Tim Tams.

Tim Tams are nothing to be scoffed at, of course; they’re Australia’s best-selling biscuit after all.

So what witchcraft recently convinced me to drop $38 for four cookies? The internet, of course.

In 2026, you’re just as likely to find entrepreneurs flogging their wares, or their cookies, on social media as you are to find them schlepping their goods at a market stall.

Flavour drops, behind-the-scenes videos, and user-generated content are how it all happens these days, and it seemed high time I got in on the action, and where better to start than with Canberra-based cookie maker Munchies?

Munchies live within the confines of Instagram with an accompanying website for ordering.

They tantalise customers with ultra close-up shots of cookies being split apart to reveal their gooey centres and flavour drops themed to occasions like Halloween … Beetlejuice cookie, anyone?

It’s sexy, almost pornographic, and very Gen Z.

I, however, am not Gen Z, but that wasn’t going to stop me from throwing a stupidly large sum of money at a promise of cookie utopia.

It might be my age bracket, or it might be poor communication, but the ordering process wasn’t exactly the smoothest. The link in the Instagram bio directed me to an ordering website where the information stated a next pickup date that was firmly in the past.

Confused, I headed back to Instagram to the post that lured me there in the first place and found that there was, in fact, an upcoming collection date a week out.

I took a punt that the website hadn’t been updated and placed my order, where I was given an address for collection but no confirmation of a collection date, just a note that I was to check Instagram stories on the day of collection.

The Biscoff cookie was the plumpest of all. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Based on the process up to that point, I wasn’t overly surprised there was no Instagram story on the specified date, so I followed my GPS deep into the burbs of Belconnen and found myself at the back door of a private townhouse, where the smell of fresh-baked cookies was unmistakable.

Turns out I should have been at the front door, but with no information stating that, and no apartment numbers on the front gates, I don’t know where that message was beamed to, but I didn’t receive it.

Frankly, at this point, it all seemed like part of the fun, like some weird cookie-themed escape room.

With the cookies nearing the cost of two bowls of pho, I decided to conduct a serious taste test and record my deep thoughts on the matter. That turned out less like an Anthony Bourdain voiceover and more like the slightly lost judges on MasterChef wondering why they have been put in charge of people’s futures.

My overarching thought was that these were some damn good cookies, and by smell alone, you could tell there were quality ingredients at work here.

Deeply buttery in aroma, dense enough to hold their shape, but lightly chewy in texture and filled to the brim with incredibly rich, gooey centres.

The dulce de leche filling in the churro-inspired cookie was a highlight, although it took me the best part of a week to get through it by cutting off small chunks to match my daily threshold for the intense sweetness.

Munchies cookie. Photo: Munchies.

Munchies cookie. Photo: Munchies.

Munchies cookie. Photo: Munchies.

Munchies cookie. Photo: Munchies.

Munchies cookie. Photo: Munchies.

Munchies cookie. Photo: Munchies.

Things get a bit meta with the Tim Tam and Biscoff-inspired cookies; a cookie flavour inspired by a biscuit flavour is a deep well that demands overanalysis. Instead, I decided to take it for what it is: a homemade cookie with a chunk of a well-known biscuit on top.

Both were exceptional.

The Tim Tam cookie eats somewhere between cookie dough and cake, and the Biscoff cookie is a plump volcano of sweet, sweet goodness.

The last in the lineup was Nutella-flavoured, and you really can’t go wrong with a cookie stuffed full of the real deal Nutella.

The one critique I had was that there was a slight texture of grainy sugar to some of the biscuits, but who am I kidding, this isn’t a CWA competition, and I didn’t seem to mind the texture when I came back four to six times a day for a week for more chunks of cookie.

So, is $38 a reasonable price to pay for four cookies? Well, there’s a recording of a mid-bite declaration calling them “freaking good cookies”. And then there’s the unreasonable number of trips I made back to the kitchen for more. So, possibly yes.

Munchies cookies are available via Instagram.

australia.title: Tears, jeers and cheers: as the Labor faithful mourn, political rivals celebrate a momentous Victorian election night
australia.snippet: Ben Carroll declares politics ‘both beautiful and brutal’ while Coalition, Greens and One Nation celebrate Full report: Victorian Coaliti...
australia.content:
“I need a beer,” the young Labor supporter said.

His mates all agreed. At the Buckley Park Bowls club in Essendon, the outgoing premier, Ben Carroll, had just given his concession speech after leading Labor to a historic wipeout.

After 12 years, Labor had been almost scrubbed off the electoral map. Carroll was among the casualties, having lost his seat of Niddrie, which the party had held for 50 years.

“As leader of the party, I take full responsibility,” he said. “Democracy is both beautiful and brutal. Beautiful, because we get to witness the will of the people. And brutal, because it is so difficult and painful to lose.”

Earlier, the mood bordered on rapturous denial. The music pumped and the beers flowed as the party faithful socialised, picking up pieces of pizza and hugging their mates.

But the small crowd was largely filled with younger Labor supporters. Former premiers Steve Bracks and John Brumby did not show. Neither did the Victorian deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, or party heavyweight and former federal cabinet member Stephen Conroy.

The Liberals had taken Mulgrave, the former seat of former premier Daniel Andrews, and the Nationals looked set to pick up Bendigo East, where former premier Jacinta Allen was retiring. On their phones to journalists, federal Labor sources rushed to distance themselves from the result.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The mood shifted when the ABC called the election for the Coalition. Voices dropped, people pulled out their phones. Voting booths had only closed at 6pm, but by 7.35 news organisations were rushing to declare a landslide result.

The vibe at the Liberal party event, in a function room at the 5-star Park Hyatt hotel on the edge of the CBD could not have been more different. There, the mood began as buzzy. As the night wore on, it shifted to jubilant.

The early arrivals chatted animatedly, drinking glasses of bubbles and nibbling at the smoked salmon tartlets and other canapés as they gathered around the massive TV screens on the walls.

When Carroll’s concession speech was broadcast, people audibly groaned as he gave an acknowledgment of country. Some booed loudly.

Coalition heavyweights, including federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor and Nationals leader, Matthew Canavan, trickled in over the course of the evening, gathering alongside Liberal supporters, many dressed in blue T-shirts.

Just before 10pm, Victoria’s new premier, Jess Wilson, entered the room to overwhelming cheers and applause. The state’s first elected female leader was swamped by rapturous supporters as she made her way to the podium.

“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it,” she told the throng. “And we will work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us.”

Across the Yarra at the Melbourne Exhibition and Convention Centre – otherwise known as “Jeff’s Shed” after former Liberal premier Jeff Kennett – One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, failed to win the seat of Pakenham, despite high expectations. This didn’t hold back the party’s federal leader, Pauline Hanson, who gave an ecstatic address.

Hanson said her party had completed its goal of having run candidates in all 88 state seats and defeated Labor and “the toxic Greens”.

It was a bold statement. By 11pm, the Greens appeared to have won eight seats while One Nation was only confirmed to have claimed only one – though a strong primary vote of about 21% had them ahead in a handful.

“They used to ignore us, but they can’t any more,” Hanson declared. “One Nation won’t be slowing down. I’m proud of what we put to Victorians this election. The major parties spent this campaign chasing focus groups. One Nation spent it saying what we believe.”

A stones throw away at the heritage-listed Mission to Seafarers Victoria building in Docklands, Greens supporters welcomed their leader, Ellen Sandell, with thunderous cheering, stomping and applause.

Anasina Gray-Barberio, a member of the Victorian Legislative Council for the northern metropolitan region, went for maximum uplift, introducing Sandell as “the legend, the diva, the queen that replaced fucking Labor”.

Sandell responded that it was the party’s most successful campaign ever and argued that for “too long we have had successive governments who’ve told us to expect less”.

“This result is not an overwhelming endorsement of the Liberals or One Nation,” she said. “This result is a rejection of the Labor party that has moved so far away from the values they once held and it is a rejection of the old party politics that just is not working for people.”

Back at the bowls club, Labor staffers kicked out the media after Carroll spoke to allow the faithful to mourn their defeat in private. Carroll’s mother Kay was walked away by friends with tears in her eyes.

Outside, it was left to an Uber driver, Jauhar, to summarise the night.

He said he had always supported Labor in the past, but this time had voted Greens. His monthly mortgage payments had risen $600 and the price of filling his petrol tank had skyrocketed. He was worried about crime, the revelations about the Big Build, and that Victoria wasn’t the state it used to be.

“We don’t expect anything good from Liberals, but maybe they can fix the corruption thing,” he said “Save some money for us Victorians.”

australia.title: Jess Wilson’s rapid rise is hard to believe - but Victorian Labor’s collapse has been years in the making
australia.snippet: Labor faces possibility of relegation to crossbench as Coalition claims majority government and Greens celebrate ‘wild’ success Full repo...
australia.content:
It is difficult to overstate how far the Victorian Coalition has come.

In the days after Christmas 2024, Brad Battin toppled John Pesutto as Liberal leader after a court found the Hawthorn MP defamed his colleague. A million-dollar loan by the party to Pesutto to help cover his legal costs also ended up in court. Battin lasted less than a year before his leadership also came undone and he was replaced by Jess Wilson in November 2025.

A year on, Wilson has become the first woman to be popularly elected as Victoria’s premier and at 36, the state’s youngest leader since federation. As of 10pm, the Coalition had won 53 seats – well above the 45 needed to form a majority government – and her Labor opponents have been wiped out, from 56 seats in 2022 to just six declared seats, according to Guardian Australia’s analysis, with a little more than a quarter of the vote counted.

The Labor leader, Ben Carroll, has secured two unwanted places in Australian political history: becoming the first premier to lose their seat at a Victorian election and the state’s shortest-serving modern premier, in the job for just 123 days.

While the final seat tally won’t be known for a few days, the Coalition has won seats in parts of the state it hasn’t ever held.

The state that had come to regard Labor as its natural party of government has consigned it to the electoral wilderness. At the current count, more people voted for One Nation across the state than Labor, with the party recording a 21% primary vote, though this did not translate into seats.

This was in part due to them overtaking Labor, on 17.6%. The Coalition’s landslide win comes off the back of a 34.78% primary vote, only a small increase from the 29.6% it recorded in its 2022 loss.

There is also a real possibility the Greens, who have won eight seats, will end up being the official opposition, with Labor consigned to the crossbench.

“It is wild, the number of seats we’re in hunt for,” the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, said on Saturday night.

It’s difficult to see how Labor will be able to rebuild into anything remotely electable in four years.

It’s hard to believe Wilson only entered parliament at the last election after the former member for Kew did not run again after a drink-driving incident in which he crashed his car into a child’s bedroom.

Immediately promoted to shadow cabinet, then to shadow treasurer and now also leader, she’s taken a party that was deeply divided and turned it into an election-winning, unified outfit.

Wilson is relatable, approachable and a small-l Liberal in a state that remains broadly progressive – if you consider the almost 20% of Victorians who voted for either the Greens or the Victorian Socialists. Much of her success can be attributed to her ability to reach beyond the Coalition’s traditional base.

Her rise has also helped attract a new calibre of candidate. She persuaded several female contenders to contest winnable seats, including Samantha Byrne, who has won Niddrie off Carroll. The party has also made a concerted effort to recruit more diverse candidates and build relationships with multicultural communities Labor has taken for granted.

In her victory speech, Wilson acknowledged it was the first time many Victorians had voted Liberals.

“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it. And we will work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us,” she said.

Wilson knows winning an election is one thing but governing is another.

Her first challenge will be translating an election victory into a mandate to govern. Many Victorians voted for change but may not know what that involves.

After all, many voters got their first meaningful taste just 48 hours before polling day, when the Coalition’s costings revealed plans to privatise or sell off around $13bn state government assets, including the state’s sewerage infrastructure.

Then, Wilson will have to manage the competing ambitions within her own ranks. She currently holds the shadow treasurer portfolio, a position several colleagues would dearly like to claim in government. She insists she intends to keep it.

The Coalition has a relatively shallow pool of experience on which to draw after 12 years in the wilderness. Bringing someone like Pesutto on to the frontbench would make sense but enrage others in the party room. It’s no wonder Wilson was tight lipped about the prospect when interviewed last month.

She described the election as a referendum on Labor. Now, she has to deliver for all those who gave her a party a chance.

Recriminations

Meanwhile, in Labor, recriminations have already started. In reality, they had weeks ago. Most of the criticism is the same – Carroll’s campaign focused too much on crime and his inability to acknowledge the 12 years of Labor that came before him – epitomised by the moment he avoided uttering Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan’s names in the debate.

But a result like this was years in the making.

After the 2022 election, Andrews vowed to do more for the communities that swung hard against Labor in the wake of the pandemic. Now, it doesn’t have one. Seats such as Kororoit, Kalkallo, Tarneit and Melton in Melbourne’s north and west and Narre Warren North in the city’s southeast, which have never been held by a party other than Labor, have turned blue.

On Saturday night, the deputy leader, Gabrielle Williams, said while the party increased seats four years ago, it ignored the main message voters were sending.

“There were certainly warning signs from the 2022 result that we should have responded to and perhaps didn’t take the opportunity,” she said.

“It should have been an inflection on point that caused us to stop and see what is happening to our base and what they weren’t getting from us.”

Labor missed another opportunity to reset when Allan became premier in 2023. “She just tried to carry on as if she was the new Daniel Andrews, it was continuation of the old government,” a campaign source said.

That government, according to the source, was bogged down by debt, alleged corruption on government construction sites, waste, crime and potholes. The potholes became daily reminders of a government that many Victorians felt was no longer delivering.

“Is there no better symbol that shows we failed to get the basics rights?” they said.

  • Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

australia.title: Victorian election 2026: Coalition wins majority government as Labor suffers historic defeat
australia.snippet: Jess Wilson to become state’s first popularly elected female premier as Ben Carroll loses seat in 2026 state election, and Greens and One...
australia.content:
Victorian Labor has suffered a historic defeat, ending 12 years of government, with the Coalition winning a majority and the Greens securing a record number of seats.

One Nation was on course to win more than 20% of the primary vote, but struggled to pick up lower house seats on a night when huge swings and three- or even four-party contests in many electorates made preference flows difficult to calculate.

At 36, Wilson will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Jacinta Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.

In her victory speech, Wilson spoke directly to Labor voters who had abandoned the party and said her team would “work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us”.

“I know that for many of you this is the first time that you have ever voted Liberal. And for others, it was the first time you have ever given us your preference,” Wilson said.

“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it.”

Carroll lost his seat of Niddrie in Melbourne’s north-western suburbs, which Labor had held for its entire 50 year history. It is the first time a Victorian premier has lost their seat at a state election.

In a speech to party faithful shortly after 8.30pm, Carroll took full responsibility for Labor’s crushing defeat.

“This is a significant loss for Labor,” Carroll said. “It’s not the result we wanted, but it is a result we accept.

“As leader of the party, I take full responsibility. Democracy is both beautiful and brutal. Beautiful, because we get to witness the will of the people. And brutal, because it is so difficult and painful to lose.

“But Victorians have spoken. And their message is clear. They want change.”

The Greens were on course to secure eight seats – holding Brunswick, Richmond and Melbourne and winning Pascoe Vale, Preston, Northcote and Footscray from Labor, and Prahran from the Liberals.

If voting trends from Saturday night’s counting continued, it appeared possible the Greens might win more lower house seats than Labor, making it the official opposition.

The party’s state leader, Ellen Sandell, told ecstatic supporters the result was “not an overwhelming endorsement of the Liberals or One Nation”.

“This result is a rejection of the Labor party that has moved so far away from the values they once held, and it is a rejection of the old party politics that just is not working for people,” Sandell said.

“We are sending more Greens to parliament than ever before at a time that could not be more crucial.

“When we say we have to replace the major parties, we are serious. It was always about more than just winning seats in parliament. It was about building a movement and a progressive political force with the courage and the conviction to stand up for what it believes.”

One Nation secured more than 20% of the statewide primary vote – up from 0.22% in 2022 – but seemed likely to gain very few lower house seats. The party is in contention the regional district of Murray Plains, held by the Nationals, and in Sunbury on Melbourne’s north-western fringe, previously held by Labor.

At One Nation Victoria’s campaign event, it was the federal leader Pauline Hanson who addressed the party faithful. The state leader, Warren Pickering, failed to win the seat of Pakenham, which went to the Liberals.

Hanson congratulated Wilson and said she “had a big job ahead of her to clear up Labor’s mess”.

“For Victoria’s sake, I wish her and her team well,” Hanson said.

One Nation’s lower house prospects appear to have been hurt by a complex preference count in Labor-held seats it targeted. As Labor fell to third place in some seats, its preferences flowed to the Liberals.

Early in the night several former Labor seats were called for the Liberals, including Frankston and Mordialloc in the south-east, Hastings on the Mornington Peninsula and Box Hill and Ringwood, in the eastern suburbs. The seat of South Barwon also went to the Liberals, the first time the party has won the seat from Labor since the 1990s.

Kororoit, Tarneit, Point Cook, Sydenham, Werribee and Melton – traditional Labor strongholds in Labor’s west and north – also fell to the Liberals.

Only about a fifth of upper house votes had been counted on Saturday night, but the Coalition looked likely to pick up at least 15 seats, with One Nation on eight and the Greens and Labor on six.

Labor MP Steve Dimopoulous, who is seen by some as a potential leader of the party if he holds on to his seat, offered a sincere apology to Labor faithful.

“This is an absolutely unequivocal report card on the Labor government,” Dimopoulous said.

The deputy Labor leader, Gabrielle Williams, another potential leadership candidate, said she was “deeply saddened” by the result and the party needed to learn from its mistakes.

“Clearly we have to be deeply humbled by the results and take the lessons from them,” Williams said.

Federal Labor sources quickly began to distance themselves from the state election result. One described the result as the “perfect storm-of-shit moment in Victoria” that would not be repeated federally.

“There are upsides federally to the Liberals being in power and cutting and privatising stuff, and One Nation’s bluster and hollowness getting tiring,” they said.

australia.title: Wilson vows to ‘bring back hope’ after historic victory in Vic election – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed. Full report: Victorian Coalition wins majority government as Labor suffers historic defeat Victoria election liv...
australia.content:
Jess Wilson claims historic victory for the Liberal party

Jess Wilson, Victoria’s first elected female premier and, at 36, one of the youngest premiers in Victorian and Australian history, is speaking to party faithful at Melbourne’s Park Hyatt, taking the stage to chants of “Jess we can”.

She entered the room to huge cheers and resounding applause, swamped by ecstatic supporters as she made her way to the stage, while the upbeat dance classic Sunchyme by the late British artist Dario G played loudly.

She says:

Thank you, my friends, and thank you, Victoria. I first want to address the people of Victoria. Thank you for the trust that you have placed in me and my team.

I know that for many of you this is the first time that you have ever voted Liberal. And for others it was the first time you have ever given us your preference. And I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it. And we will work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us.

I know that you have elected me to bring back hope to this state. And that is what I pledge to do, starting from tomorrow.

    Welcome

What we learned, Victorian election night 2026

It’s been a long evening and the results will continue to roll in over coming days – and undoubtedly there will be surprises to come – but this is where we’re going to leave our live coverage for the evening.

Here’s a summary of what’s occurred today:

  • Victorian Labor has suffered a historic state election defeat, its 12 years in power ending, as the Coalition takes majority government.

  • Labor leader and premier Ben Carroll has not only lost the election for Labor, but also lost his own seat of Niddrie.

  • Jess Wilson, Victoria’s first elected female premier and one of the youngest premiers in Victorian and Australian history, claimed victory for the Liberal party.

  • Carroll says the Labor party will need to do a lot of listening from here on if it is to win back the trust of the public.

  • Greens leader Ellen Sandell celebrated party’s ‘wild’ success as they look set to pick up eight lower house seats – a record for the party in Victoria.

  • A Coalition government seems likely to be negotiating in the upper house with either a One Nation bloc or with a combined Greens and Labor bloc to pass legislation.

  • Labor figures are already beginning to call for an end to the factional games that have plagued the party in recent years and played a role in its recent failures.

  • One Nation looks on track to win at least two seats, but state leader Warren Pickering has failed to win the seat of Pakenham.

Thanks so much for your company this evening. Good night.

And if you want to catch up on Jess Wilson’s victory speech for the Liberal party, you can see it here:

Bertin Huynh

Celebrating with the Greens rank and file is former leader Samantha Ratnam. She was happy about the night’s result and said the party was there “to offer a vision of hope”

“We’re making breakthroughs,” said Ratnam referring to the swathe of new Greens MPs that were elected tonight.

We’re ready to take on the establishment parties and we got to support people material needs and we got to protect our environment.

On Victoria’s treaty with its Indigenous peoples, she said:

Victorian community is going to come out in droves to say they don’t want the first treaty in Australia to be ripped to shreds.

If you missed Ben Carroll’s concession speech this evening, you can watch it here:

Henry Belot

‘We don’t even know who the opposition is going to be’ – Jane Hume

Victorian senator and deputy leader of the federal Liberals, Jane Hume, says her colleagues will study the state result closely but cautions against expecting similar results in New South Wales or nationally.

Hume says:

We don’t even know who the opposition is going to be. At this stage, it might not be Labor. That is quite extraordinary. Every election is different. We will take the lessons of this election and I think that Victorian Labor, what’s left of it, will be as well.

Greens leader Ellen Sandell celebrates 'wild' success

Bertin Huynh

The Greens have welcomed their leader Ellen Sandell with thunderous cheering, stomping and applause to celebrates what she describes as the party’s “most successful campaign” in the state’s history, winning “more seats than One Nation”.

The Docklands event has been lively. When the ABC called Pascoe Vale for the Greens, chants of sheer joy erupted. Then, when premier-elect Jess Wilson appeared on screen, boos could be heard from the crowd. When Pauline Hanson appeared, booing and rude gestures were made at the TV screens.

The MC of the night, MLC candidate for northern metro, Anasina Gray-Barberio introducing Sandell as “as the legend, the diva, the queen, that replaced fucking Labor”.

To the group of estatic Greens members and supporters, Sandell said:

For too long we have had successive governments who’ve told us to expect less.

This result is not an overwhelming endorsement of the Liberals or One nation. This result is a rejection of the Labor Party that has moved so far away from the values they once held, and it is a rejection of the old party politics that just is not working for people.

We are sending more Greens to parliament than ever before at a time that could not be more crucial.

A crowd of candidates joined Sandell on the stage alongside federal leader David Shoebridge, as Sandell said: “it is wild the number of seats we’re in hunt for.”

When we say we have to replace the major parties we are serious. It was always about more than just winning seats in Parliament. It was about building a movement and a progressive political force with the courage and the conviction to stand up for what it believes it for.

Shoebridge said:

This Green wave has been built on hope. We’re not here for managed decline. The Greens are here to say better times are ahead.

He vowed to take the “green wave” across the country.

What is happening with the upper house?

Nick Evershed

Some results are in for the legislative council, and the Coalition have nine seats, One Nation six, and then Labor and Greens with three apiece.

The Coalition are looking likely for at least another five, which would put them on 14, which would not give them a majority in the upper house, even if they win a few more.

This makes it likely that a Coalition government will be negotiating with either a One Nation bloc to pass legislation, or with a combined Greens and Labor bloc.

One Nation's Warren Pickering fails to win Pakenham – ABC

Henry Belot

The ABC says One Nation Victoria’s leader, Warren Pickering, has failed to win the seat of Pakenham.

Here’s the national broadcaster’s election analyst Casey Briggs:

One Nation is getting a strong primary, but they’re not going to make it into parliament in many, or most of those seats, because preferences are not going to be their friends.

Warren Pickering will not be in parliament, the member for Pakenham will be a Liberal.

Henry Belot

Loyal Victorian Labor staffers are devastated by tonight’s result. Former senior staffers have unloaded on the party’s campaign and its strategy.

One Labor source says there is “genuine dismay that the Government’s many achievements, including the construction of 121 schools, were not featured more prominently in Labor’s campaign”.

Former staffers are also dismayed by how diabolically bad Labor’s election campaign has been, with crime and the Big Build royal commission featuring prominently, strongly reinforcing the Coalition’s messages.

The premier has been portrayed as basically a decent bloke who inherited a mess. This overlooks that his communication throughout the campaign has been poor, he was a minister for around 10 years – including deputy premier – and is also a creature of the factions and backroom deals.

Another former Labor staffer said:

This is what happens when you forget that government is a privilege, not a right.

Greens projected to secure eight seats in inner Melbourne

Nick Evershed

The Greens are doing very well tonight, picking up at least four seats so far from Labor, bringing their total to eight overall:

This is up from four seats in 2022, making it a significant gain for the party. This result will also be a historic high point for the party in the state.

Labor with some more runs on the board

Nick Evershed

The Labor party are finally getting some more runs on the board with the latest round of seat calls. We’re projecting a Labor win in the following seats:

Ivanhoe – ALP
Mill Park – ALP
Thomastown – ALP
Williamstown – ALP
Greenvale – ALP

‘We can’t fix Victoria overnight’: Wilson

Wilson is coming to the denouement of her speech (she has been speaking for more than 15 minutes now). After numerous thank-yous, she comes back to the party’s drubbing of Labor:

Friends, I have said many times that we can’t fix Victoria overnight. It will take years of hard work and responsible governing to get Victoria back to the place it used to be. A place where people felt hopeful and optimistic, where they felt safe and content.

But I want to make a commitment tonight. Labor have failed many times over 12 years, but their chief failure was that they stopped trusting the Victorian people with the truth.

Victorians have placed their trust in me tonight and I will always return that trust with the truth. That’s my commitment. That’s the kind of premier I want to be. The kind of premier who is honest from day one.

Wilson: Liberal party’s ‘last rites were premature’

Jess Wilson, still addressing the party faithful, alludes to the fact that for a long time and until not very long ago, the Liberal Party’s prospects of winning back government in Victoria seemed out of the question.

She says:

A lot has been said about the future of the Liberal Party. Tonight, we showed that those last rites were premature.

We showed that when you put in the work, you listen to the Victorian people, and you put forward a plan that will deliver hope for this state, you can win, and we did win.

Wilson thanks ‘decent man’ Ben Carroll after outgoing premier called to concede

Jess Wilson says she received a call from outgoing premier Ben Carroll earlier this evening.

He graciously congratulated me and the Liberal and Nationals team. He has served Victoria at the highest levels – as a minister, as deputy premier and as premier. Taking on the leadership of the state in difficult circumstances. Ben is a decent man, and I wish his family well for what lies next.

But today, Victorians have drawn a line in the sand after 12 long years. Victorians have sent a clear message that they cannot allow the state to continue on the direction it has been going in under Labor. Victorians want a fresh start.

I’m incredibly proud of the positive plan we have put to the Victorian people at this election. And now we have the mandate that we need to get started.

‘We will not let you down’: Wilson

Wilson continues her victory speech:

Earlier this year I travelled the length and breadth of this great state. Everywhere I went people told me that they needed a fresh start. And as I stand here tonight, I am deeply grateful to have earned the trust of the Victorian people to deliver that fresh start.

I am very conscious of the great privilege pledge and the weight of responsibility that has been placed upon me and my entire team tonight. To those who placed their faith in the Liberal and National parties tonight, I will not let you down. We will not let you down.

To those who did not, rest assured, I will govern for all Victorians. I will govern for all Victorians and in the best interests of Victoria every day.

Jess Wilson claims historic victory for the Liberal party

Jess Wilson, Victoria’s first elected female premier and, at 36, one of the youngest premiers in Victorian and Australian history, is speaking to party faithful at Melbourne’s Park Hyatt, taking the stage to chants of “Jess we can”.

She entered the room to huge cheers and resounding applause, swamped by ecstatic supporters as she made her way to the stage, while the upbeat dance classic Sunchyme by the late British artist Dario G played loudly.

She says:

Thank you, my friends, and thank you, Victoria. I first want to address the people of Victoria. Thank you for the trust that you have placed in me and my team.

I know that for many of you this is the first time that you have ever voted Liberal. And for others it was the first time you have ever given us your preference. And I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it. And we will work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us.

I know that you have elected me to bring back hope to this state. And that is what I pledge to do, starting from tomorrow.

Coalition's primary vote has actually gone down

Luke Mansillo

The Coalition’s primary vote is actually down compared with 2022, so how are they doing so well in winning seats?

The Liberal party’s primary vote is down by about 1 percentage point, but they’ve managed to secure enough seats to form government.

Meanwhile, Labor’s primary vote is down by 19 percentage points, and One Nation has gained 21 percentage points, albeit off a base of almost zero votes in 2022.

The Coalition has produced an incredibly efficient geographic distribution of votes, managing to stay just ahead of enough candidates to be the beneficiary of the preferential system.

Greens and Victorian Socialist voters prefer the Liberals over One Nation, and with Labor being knocked out quite early in the count, the Liberal party is mopping up preferences from the left of politics.

Nick Evershed

Seats to watch: Bendigo West

We think that there is a possibility that Bendigo West could end up as a competition between the Greens and One Nation, making this an interesting one to watch.

The reason is that after the Animal Justice party and Victorian Socialists are excluded in the fifth and sixth positions, that allows the Greens to leapfrog Labor. One Nation may benefit from Family First voter preferences, allowing them to get ahead of the Nationals.

However, it’s also possible that when early votes are counted, the Nationals stay ahead. All of this makes for a complicated race to call.

world.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
world.snippet: What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural land...
world.content:
As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.

“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.

Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.

Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.

“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.

“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

world.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
world.snippet: The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid? Lana Nussei...
world.content:
Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.

The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.

“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.

The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.

A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”

That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.

Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

world.title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
world.snippet: Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 21 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred A crash involving a fu...
world.content:
A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.

State media reported that the fire broke out when the fuel truck overturned. The stretch of the highway where it occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the health ministry said.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene.

Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.

“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he said, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.”

The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further. He later travelled to the scene and to the hospitals, the health ministry said.

The minister’s spokesperson told the state-linked Al-Qahera News that the ring road had been reopened and the remnants of the accident cleared.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January 2016, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

world.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
world.snippet: Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park A Swiss touri...
world.content:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

world.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
world.snippet: Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections The UK sent a Sri La...
world.content:
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”

Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.

Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.
